title: 22 years later, retired MV-22 pilot climbs back into the Osprey
summary: Col Chris “Mongo” Seymour flew the U.S. Marine Corps variant of the V-22 into its first combat deployment in Iraq in 2008.
body_markdown:
Col Chris “Mongo” Seymour, USMC (Ret.) had a military career spanning decades which included being one of the early test pilots of the V-22 in the late 1990s, flying the U.S. Marine Corps variant of the V-22 (MV-22) into its first combat deployment in Iraq (2008), before officially retiring from service in 2013.


“It’s like the Swiss Army knife you didn’t know you needed until you had it in a bind,” said Seymour. “The later production lot aircraft are exponentially better than the V-22s that I flew in the 90s and early 2000s.”


For the past 13 years, Seymour has served in leadership roles in aerospace and defense manufacturing.


When given the opportunity to test fly a new production MV-22 in the summer of 2026, he was eager to take his “dream shot.”


“When I got the opportunity, it was like a dream come true. I mean, it’s like winning the lottery,” Seymour exclaimed. “But flying the MV-22 to the Marine Corps was just way too cool to pass up.”


Bell Photo


In July 2026, Bell Textron celebrated a production milestone for the MV-22 Program of Record with a ceremony at the Bell Amarillo Assembly Center. The United States Marine Corps operates the largest fleet with 359 MV-22 aircraft produced and delivered into service.


“It’s a game changer. It was ahead of its time 30 years ago, and it’s still ahead of everybody else,” continued Seymour. “The V-22 processing speed is fast; it’s kept pace with technology. Operating the V-22, and tilt-rotor technology in combat has literally saved thousands of lives!”


With the achievement of the MV-22 POR milestone, Team Osprey — the group of industry partners consisting of more than 500 US-based suppliers and 27,000 employees from across 44 states — is now focused on fleet wide sustainment and upgrades to meet the USMC’s expectation of having the MV-22 Osprey fleet flying until 2055.


Bell and Boeing continue to build new CMV-22 variants for the U.S Navy and support the Nacelle Improvement modernization program for the U.S. Air Force CV-22 fleet.


*This press release was prepared and distributed by Bell.*
